scenarios.title: Who is on my team?
scenarios.objective: Find a teammate before choosing whom to involve.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have the puck in a sharing activity. Navy2 wears navy like you; Gold1 wears gold. The coach asks you to find your teammate. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU and Navy2 are navy.
Gold1 is gold.
YOU have the puck.

questions.prompt: Who is your teammate?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is on the same navy team as YOU. The labels also identify the teams.

questions.prompt: Which two things can you find here?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is your teammate and YOU have the puck. No goal has happened.

questions.prompt: Put this sharing routine in order.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested routine. Matching jerseys alone does not make a pass safe.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little nearer Navy2 without standing on Navy2.
questions.explanation: This example shortens the distance while keeping separate space. Other clear starting spots could work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 steps between you and Navy2. What could you do?

options.text: Shoot the puck away without looking for Navy2

questions.explanation: A teammate can become covered. Look again or find clearer space. Sending the puck away before you look can give Gold1 a chance to get it.

questions.prompt: Tell a grown-up how you found your teammate.
questions.explanation: Mention navy, the Navy2 label or the team introduction. Pointing is fine.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 takes the puck from YOU. What should you notice first?

options.text: Can I pass the old way?

questions.explanation: Gold1 now has the puck, so YOU must notice the change before deciding what to do. YOU cannot keep passing as though the puck were still yours.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 moves to a new spot while YOU hold the puck. Which two players should YOU keep track of?

options.text: Gold1, who may block the way
Only where Navy2 used to stand

questions.explanation: Check where Navy2 is now and where Gold1 is before choosing a pass. A teammate’s old spot may no longer be useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU with the puck to try a different passing angle toward Navy2.
questions.explanation: Try a controlled move that leaves a clear path toward Navy2 while keeping Gold1 in view. The puck stays with YOU. This is one example to discuss, not the only place that can work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 skates closer to YOU. Tell an adult what changed.
questions.explanation: A useful answer names Gold1 as closer pressure and Navy2 as a teammate to find. The next puck touch should follow that new picture.

scenarios.title: A puck with nobody holding it
scenarios.objective: Tell a loose puck from a carried puck.
scenarios.briefing: The coach placed a puck in a quiet practice area. Nobody controls it yet. Navy2 waits beside the area. YOU are invited to collect it. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The puck is separate from both players.
Navy2 is waiting.
YOU are invited to collect.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck right now?
questions.explanation: The setup has no puck owner. It is between the players.

questions.prompt: What did the coach ask YOU to do?
questions.explanation: That is the instruction in the briefing.

questions.prompt: Arrange a gentle collection try.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested practice sequence; the picture does not measure skating or control.

questions.prompt: Show a place near the puck to finish your approach.
questions.explanation: The reference approaches without going far beyond the puck. Several nearby places may suit the activity.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 reaches it first and controls it. Is it still loose?

options.text: Only until YOU skate over to it

questions.explanation: A puck is loose until a player controls it. Once Navy2 controls it in the stated event, it is not loose, even if another player is skating toward it.

questions.prompt: How could you tell the puck was waiting for someone?
questions.explanation: Point to the separate puck and notice that neither player controls it.

questions.prompt: After YOU collect it, Navy2 asks for a pass. What helps before sending it?

options.text: Look to see if Navy2 is ready
Pass at once because you heard a call
Keep looking only at your stick

questions.explanation: A call helps you find Navy2. Look up and check that your partner is ready before passing.

questions.prompt: After the pickup, what helps a pass reach Navy2?

options.text: Aim where Navy2 stood before moving

questions.explanation: Find the partner and their ready stick. If Navy2 moves, the old spot may no longer be a useful target.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to give YOU a short pass after the pickup. Leave room between you.
questions.explanation: This brings Navy2 onto a shorter passing line from the pickup area. A different clear target can work if both players are ready.

questions.prompt: You touched the puck, but it slid away. Is your pickup finished? Tell a grown-up.
questions.explanation: Touching the puck once is different from controlling it. Find it again, approach under control, and keep it close enough for your next touch.

scenarios.title: Room to carry
scenarios.objective: Notice an occupied route and a roomier practice area.
scenarios.briefing: YOU hold the puck. Gold1 is directly ahead. Navy2 waits off to one side. The coach invites you to explore the empty side away from Navy2. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 is ahead of YOUR facing direction.
Navy2 occupies one side of the practice area.
The opposite side has no player.

questions.prompt: Who is directly ahead of YOU?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is ahead in the direction YOU face.

questions.prompt: What is shown on the side away from Navy2?
questions.explanation: No player is placed on that side of the activity. Empty space does not guarantee an escape.

questions.prompt: Arrange this try at finding room.

options.text: Carry a short way and look again

questions.explanation: The routine invites another look when the situation changes.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into the empty practice space away from Navy2.
questions.explanation: This leaves the crowded line and the side Navy2 occupies. Other clear places may fit; a real route still needs checking.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 moves into that empty space. What could you do?
questions.explanation: Notice the new player position instead of remembering one fixed spot.

questions.prompt: Point to one thing you checked before carrying.
questions.explanation: Gold1, Navy2 or the empty ice are relevant observations. Speaking or pointing is enough.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 covers your first angle, what should Navy2 see?

options.text: A different clear target or lane

questions.explanation: Gold1 removed the first window. A new angle or lane gives Navy2 a real choice if it is visible.

questions.prompt: After moving, what two players should YOU check?

options.text: Navy2, who is waiting for a pass

questions.explanation: YOU have the puck, so YOU choose the next play. Navy2 is the teammate who could receive it, and Gold1 could change the way there. Only the players in this picture can be checked.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in a spot where the way to Navy2 stays open.
questions.explanation: This spot keeps the way to Navy2 open and is closer to your partner than the empty-side example. Gold1 is still ahead in the middle, so check the way again after any move. Other open spots can work; the test is whether the path to Navy2 stays clear.

questions.prompt: Imagine YOU pass to Navy2 and Navy2 now has the puck. How can you show you are ready for a return pass?
questions.explanation: This is a stated change: in the picture YOU still have the puck. After a pass, moving where Navy2 can see you and keeping your stick ready are ways to show it. Whether a return pass fits still depends on where Gold1 is.

scenarios.title: From the boards to the circle
scenarios.objective: Use boards and faceoff circle to understand a practice instruction.
scenarios.briefing: YOU are near the side boards. The coach names the nearby red ring a faceoff circle and asks you to return to its middle for the next turn. Navy2 waits outside the circle. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The boards are near YOU.
The named circle is centred near x=20.7, y=6.7.
Navy2 waits outside the circle.

questions.prompt: What does the coach call the nearby red ring?
questions.explanation: The briefing names this painted ring. It is a landmark in this practice.

questions.prompt: Where are YOU starting?
questions.explanation: YOU are close to the side boards and outside the painted circle.

questions.prompt: Arrange the return to our practice spot.

options.text: Check that the space is clear

questions.explanation: This is a suggested activity reset, not a faceoff rule or skating test.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle of that faceoff circle.
questions.explanation: The reference is the stated practice spot. The coach could accept a nearby clear place; no tactical optimality is claimed.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 stands in the middle first. What could you do?
questions.explanation: Give your partner room and follow the coach's next instruction. Skating into the spot anyway, or moving your partner out of it, takes the turn from them.

questions.prompt: Point to the boards, then point to the circle.
questions.explanation: Recognizing the two named areas is the aim. A point or spoken answer is enough.

questions.prompt: While YOU wait for your turn, what helps YOU look after the puck?

options.text: Keep it close to your stick
Leave it in the middle of the circle

questions.explanation: YOU are carrying the puck while Navy2 uses the circle. Keeping it close means it is ready when your turn comes and it stays out of your partner’s space. A coach may instead ask players to set their pucks aside for a turn; sending it away can also mean chasing it later.

questions.prompt: Before leaving the boards for your turn, what should YOU check?

options.text: Where the coach asked you to go
Whether the way there is clear
Whether you can beat Navy2 to the spot

questions.explanation: Find the named practice spot and check your route. Getting there first is not the aim of this reset.

questions.prompt: For another waiting spot, move Navy2 outside the circle on its centre-ice side.
questions.explanation: This waiting spot stays outside the painted circle and gives the next player room. The coach can choose another clear waiting place.

questions.prompt: Can you skate across the painted circle line to reach the middle? What should you look for?
questions.explanation: The circle is paint on the ice, not a wall. You can cross it in this activity after checking the way is clear and it is your turn.

scenarios.title: Listen for the practice stop
scenarios.objective: Recognize a stated practice stop signal.
scenarios.briefing: In this practice only, one whistle means stop under control and listen. It has just sounded. YOU hold the puck; Navy2 uses a separate lane. This is not a match restart rule. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: A practice stop signal was stated.
YOU own the puck.
The players have separate lanes.

questions.prompt: What does this practice whistle mean?
questions.explanation: The briefing defines the signal for this activity.

questions.prompt: Which things help after that signal?
questions.explanation: Listening and awareness fit the instruction. These are suggested behaviours.

questions.prompt: Order this practice stop.
questions.explanation: The picture cannot measure stopping distance or technique.

questions.prompt: Is stopping the same as skating faster?

options.text: Yes, they both use your edges
Only when you are going fast

questions.explanation: Stopping and speeding up both use your edges, but they are different actions with different jobs. This practice signal asks for stopping under control.

questions.prompt: Now the coach invites a restart in your lane. What could you do?

options.text: Check the lane and begin gently
Start before the coach finishes talking
Assume every whistle has the same meaning

questions.explanation: Follow the new instruction. Waiting until the coach finishes and checking your own lane keeps the restart safe for both players. Another activity may use different signals.

questions.prompt: Tell a grown-up what you would listen for next.
questions.explanation: The next instruction or permission to begin is relevant. An adult can record spoken words.

questions.prompt: You have stopped, but the puck slides away. What could YOU do while the coach is talking?

options.text: Listen and ask before going to get it
Ask Navy2 to race after it

questions.explanation: Stay with the stop-and-listen instruction. Ask for help collecting the puck rather than starting another chase.

questions.prompt: Before turning to listen, what helps YOU give Navy2 room?

options.text: Keep your stick in your own space

questions.explanation: Notice your partner while you turn and leave room for both players and their sticks.

questions.prompt: The coach asks Navy2 to use more space for the next try. Move Navy2 farther from YOUR lane.
questions.explanation: This separates the two practice lanes. It is a new coach-directed setup, not permission to restart before the next signal.

questions.prompt: You did not hear what the coach said next. What could you say?
questions.explanation: Try “Can you say that again?” or “Can you show me?” Asking helps you know when and where to start the next try.

scenarios.title: Ready for a short pass
scenarios.objective: Recognize the invited receiver and a partner-passing setup.
scenarios.briefing: Navy2 holds the puck for a gentle partner pass. YOU wait at an angle. Gold1 stands outside this first activity and is not challenging. No pass has happened yet. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Navy2 has the puck.
YOU are the invited receiver.
Gold1 is not challenging this try.

questions.prompt: Who starts with the puck?
questions.explanation: The puck is attached to Navy2.

questions.prompt: What is YOUR job in this activity?

options.text: Skate over and take the puck from Navy2
Wait with your back to Navy2

questions.explanation: The briefing identifies YOU as the receiver. Taking the puck from your partner, or turning away from them, would end the partner pass before it starts.

questions.prompt: Arrange a simple partner pass.

options.text: Get ready for the gentle pass

questions.explanation: This is a suggested progression. The eventual pass needs its own explicit movement; it is not shown yet.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little nearer, leaving space between partners.
questions.explanation: This example shortens the distance. Other clear receiving places could work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 is not ready yet. What could you do?
questions.explanation: You can wait or communicate instead of forcing the activity.

questions.prompt: How could you show your partner you are ready?
questions.explanation: A clear look or simple call can help. Discuss a receiving target with the coach; no physical technique is graded.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2’s pass slides a little behind YOU. What could YOU do?

options.text: Turn and skate to the puck under control
Wait for Navy2 to come and get it
Reach across without moving your feet

questions.explanation: Missing the first touch is normal in practice. Turning and going to the puck keeps the activity going. Reaching without moving your feet often puts you off balance, and waiting leaves the puck where it stopped. Nothing in this picture shows how hard or how fast a pass would be.

questions.prompt: Which two things can YOU see that help YOU get ready?

options.text: The ice between YOU and Navy2 is open

questions.explanation: The picture shows Navy2 with the puck and no player between the partners. The player artwork does not establish a reliable shooting-hand cue for this question.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a second waiting spot that keeps the ice to Navy2 open.
questions.explanation: No player stands between this spot and Navy2, and Navy2 would not have to turn far to see YOU. Gold1 is not part of this try, so the choice is about staying visible to your partner. Other open spots can work; the test is whether the ice between the partners stays clear.

questions.prompt: Gold1 is not in this try. What would change if Gold1 joined in?
questions.explanation: With nobody challenging, YOU can pick a waiting spot mainly for a clear view of Navy2. If someone joined in, YOU would also check where they are and whether the ice between the partners is still open. This picture does not show that change, so any answer about it is a discussion, not something the scene proves.

scenarios.title: My turn to defend the goal
scenarios.objective: Recognize the goal-defending turn and nearby crease.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have a short turn defending the navy goal at the -x end. The coach names the blue area in front of the net the crease. You are a skater taking a turn, not a permanent goalie. Gold1 has the puck; Navy2 takes the next turn. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU are assigned the navy goal at the -x end.
The blue area is named the crease.
Navy2 is next in the rotation.

questions.prompt: Which goal are YOU defending?

options.text: The gold goal at the +x end
The navy goal at the -x end

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns YOU the navy goal at the -x end for this turn.

questions.prompt: What did the coach call the blue area by the net?
questions.explanation: The name is given in the briefing. This identifies an area, not a crease-entry rule.

questions.prompt: Arrange our goal-defending turns.
questions.explanation: This is the declared rotation; the coach controls the swap.

questions.prompt: Which facts belong to this activity?
questions.explanation: Gold1 owns the puck and Navy2 is next. The role is shared.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 gains control of the puck. Who has it then?
questions.explanation: The answer follows the stated change of possession.

questions.prompt: How could you help Navy2 enjoy the next turn?
questions.explanation: Encouragement and room to try are useful answers. No goaltending technique is scored.

questions.prompt: It is YOUR turn near the navy net. Where should YOU look first?

options.text: At the far end of the rink

questions.explanation: Gold1 has the puck near your net, so watch Gold1 and the puck. If Navy2 gains control, follow the puck to Navy2 and check what happens next. The play may still be near your net.

questions.prompt: Which two things tell YOU where the play is right now?

options.text: How close the puck is to the navy net
Who takes the next turn after YOU

questions.explanation: The puck owner and how close the puck is to your net tell YOU what is happening now. Who takes the next turn matters between turns, not during this one.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a spot in front of the navy net where you can still see the puck.
questions.explanation: From here YOU stay in front of the navy net and can still see Gold1 and the puck. It is one example spot, and where you stand changes as the puck moves. This is an activity suggestion, not goaltending technique.

questions.prompt: Why does everyone get a turn defending the goal?
questions.explanation: Sharing the turn lets every player practise many parts of the game instead of only one. Any answer in your own words is fine, and nothing here is scored.

scenarios.title: A teammate behind your shoulder
scenarios.objective: Look beyond the forward direction to find a teammate.
scenarios.briefing: YOU face the attacking end and hold the puck. Navy2 is behind your facing direction. Gold1 is ahead on the other side. The coach asks you to find Navy2 before deciding on a puck action. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU face +x.
Navy2 is behind that facing direction.
Finding Navy2 does not prove a pass is open.

questions.prompt: Where is Navy2 compared with the way YOU face?
questions.explanation: YOU face the attacking end while Navy2 is behind YOU.

questions.prompt: What can looking around help you find?
questions.explanation: Teammate locations and pressure are the source-supported information cues.

questions.prompt: Arrange this looking activity.

options.text: Tell the coach where Navy2 is

questions.explanation: This is the activity routine. A screen answer does not demonstrate a real shoulder check.

questions.prompt: For a second try, move YOU away from the side with Navy2.
questions.explanation: This changes the viewing relationship while leaving space. It is a practice reset, not an ideal game position.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 skates ahead of YOU. Should you keep pointing behind?
questions.explanation: Locate the teammate again when their position changes.

questions.prompt: Point to one thing you might miss by only watching the puck.
questions.explanation: Navy2 is a concrete example. A spoken answer or pointing is enough.

questions.prompt: Gold1 moves into the way ahead. What could YOU look for behind your shoulder?

options.text: Navy2 and a clear way to pass

questions.explanation: Navy2 is behind YOU. Looking there can reveal a different choice, but you still need a clear passing lane.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check before a pass back to Navy2?

options.text: Whether Gold1 can reach the passing lane
Only which way YOUR skates point

questions.explanation: A teammate behind you can help if you locate the target and check the lane. Facing forward does not remove the option of a pass back.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to a new waiting place behind YOU, with room for a short pass.
questions.explanation: Navy2 stays behind the way YOU face and separate from YOUR spot. Several nearby places can give a different passing angle.

questions.prompt: Why might a short pass back to Navy2 help you go forward later?
questions.explanation: It can move the puck away from Gold1’s pressure and give your team another view of the space ahead. Passing back is useful when that lane is clear; you do not have to use it every time.

scenarios.title: My partner has it now
scenarios.objective: Recognize the new puck owner after a completed partner pass.
scenarios.briefing: A gentle partner pass has finished. Navy2 controls the puck; YOU no longer do. This picture begins after reception and does not show the pass path. Leave Navy2 room while staying in the activity. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Navy2 owns the puck.
YOU are now without it.
The earlier pass is stated, not animated.

questions.prompt: Who controls the puck now?
questions.explanation: The setup begins with the puck controlled by Navy2.

questions.prompt: Does this picture show the whole moving pass?
questions.explanation: The briefing limits it to the state after reception.

questions.prompt: Put these stated events in order.
questions.explanation: This is the supplied history, not an independently simulated pass.

questions.prompt: Find separate space where Navy2 can still see YOU.
questions.explanation: This gives Navy2 room and leaves a visible partner. Other clear places may fit.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 asks for a return target. What could you do?
questions.explanation: You can stay involved by getting available. A return pass still needs a clear route.

questions.prompt: What changed for YOU when the pass finished?
questions.explanation: YOU changed from having the puck to being without it. You can still help the activity.

questions.prompt: Gold1 skates closer to Navy2. What could YOU do to stay useful?

options.text: Find open space where Navy2 could reach YOU with a pass
Skate straight at Navy2 to take the puck back
Stand still until someone calls your name

questions.explanation: Navy2 has the puck and Gold1 is the pressure. Open space gives Navy2 a choice. It only becomes a pass if the route from Navy2 to YOU stays clear.

questions.prompt: Which two things should YOU watch now that Navy2 has the puck?

options.text: Where Navy2 is on the ice
Where the puck was before the pass

questions.explanation: Your teammate and the pressure are the two cues that change what YOU do next. Where the puck used to be can be useful context, but checking Navy2 and Gold1 tells YOU what matters now.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in open space where Navy2 could pass to YOU, away from Gold1.
questions.explanation: From here YOU are on the opposite side from Gold1 with a short open route to the puck. It is one example spot; another open place can work, and a pass still depends on that route staying clear.

questions.prompt: Why does Navy2 need room after taking the pass?
questions.explanation: Standing too close takes away the space Navy2 needs to carry the puck, and it can bring Gold1 to both of you at once. Any answer in your own words is fine.

scenarios.title: A mistake and another try
scenarios.objective: Respond kindly to a teammate error while noticing possession.
scenarios.briefing: In a friendly keep-away activity, Navy2 missed a pass and Gold1 gained the puck. The picture starts after that change. Navy2 looks to YOU for encouragement; the coach invites everyone to keep trying. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 owns the puck now.
The missed pass was described.
Everyone is invited to try again.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck after the missed pass?

questions.prompt: For the next reset, find separate practice space near Navy2.

questions.prompt: Gold1 has the puck now. What is a good first thing for YOU to do?

options.text: Notice who has the puck and where Navy2 is
Wait for the coach to tell YOU what happened
Skate to where the pass was going

questions.explanation: The puck changed hands, so the old plan is finished. Noticing the new owner and where your teammate is gives YOU something useful to do next.

questions.prompt: Which two things are true in this picture?

options.text: The pass to Navy2 did not finish
YOU are the navy player closest to the puck

questions.explanation: The picture starts after the miss, with Gold1 holding the puck. Navy2 is actually the navy player nearer the puck, so the third choice does not match what YOU can see.

questions.prompt: Place YOU in open space where Navy2 can find YOU for the next try.
questions.explanation: This gives YOU room on the far side from Gold1 and a short open route to Navy2 for the next try. It is one example spot; another open place can work. The picture does not prove Navy2 has already looked at YOU.

questions.prompt: What does “another try” mean after a missed pass?
questions.explanation: It means noticing what is true now, that Gold1 has the puck and Navy2 does not, and then getting ready to help again. Repeating the old pass plan without looking ignores where Gold1 is. Any answer in your own words is fine.

questions.prompt: Why keep your feet moving toward room?

questions.prompt: Which player is closer to the middle of the ice than YOU?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is nearer the middle. Navy2 is closer to the side boards. Check Gold1 before moving toward the middle.

questions.prompt: What can help protect the puck?

options.text: Keep your body between Gold1 and the puck
Send the puck up the wall without looking

questions.explanation: Keeping your body between Gold1 and the puck can help protect it. Looking for Navy2 helps YOU decide whether a pass is available. Sending the puck along the wall without checking can give Gold1 a chance to reach it.

questions.prompt: Place YOU a little closer to the wall side, away from Gold1.

questions.prompt: Put the protection read in order.

options.text: Keep the puck on the far side
Look for Navy2 or new room

questions.explanation: The defender's side tells you where the first pressure is. Protect there, then scan for a teammate or a better lane.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 reaches the wall side too. What is a smart update?

options.text: Look for another lane before carrying on
Keep the puck there without looking
Send the pass to Navy2 without checking the lane

questions.explanation: Imagine Gold1 moving toward the wall side. Check how much room and reach Gold1 has now. A turn, a clear pass to Navy2 or protecting the puck may help; the next choice depends on what is still open.

questions.prompt: Why keep the puck away from Gold1?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is inside YOU, so the puck is easier to reach there. Keeping your body between the defender and puck can buy a moment to see Navy2 or another lane.

questions.prompt: What is between Navy2 and YOUR current spot?

options.text: Open ice with nobody in it

questions.explanation: Gold1 lies on the straight line joining Navy2 and YOU, so that lane is not open.

questions.prompt: Which cues matter before asking for a pass?
questions.explanation: Check Navy2 with the puck and where Gold1 is now. Your earlier spot can help YOU notice what changed, but it does not tell YOU whether the lane is clear now.

questions.prompt: Move YOU away from the boards toward a clearer window near the faceoff circle.
questions.explanation: This example moves off the blocked line. Other open windows may work. A static line does not certify a moving pass.

questions.prompt: Arrange one way to become a target.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested support routine; timing and defender response still need review.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 follows into your new window. What might help?

options.text: Stand still because the circle is the named spot
Ask for the same blocked pass

questions.explanation: The circle is a useful landmark, not a guaranteed correct position.

questions.prompt: How did leaving the boards change the passing picture?
questions.explanation: Explain the change in angle relative to Navy2 and Gold1. Another clear angle can be a reasonable answer.

questions.prompt: No window opens for YOU right now. What is a fair read?

options.text: Navy2 can keep the puck or move while YOU keep working for space
Navy2 has to pass right away
YOU should skate straight back to the boards

questions.explanation: A pass is not owed on every play. Navy2 can hold or carry the puck while YOU keep working for a visible angle, and Gold1's position decides when a lane opens.

questions.prompt: What two players must YOU read after moving?
questions.explanation: Navy2 decides whether a pass is available, and Gold1 can close the new angle. Both positions shape the next read.

questions.prompt: Place YOU closer to Navy2 for a shorter pass, off the boards.
questions.explanation: This example is near support: a shorter angle from a spot away from the boards, with Gold1 well off that lane. A farther window such as the circle area can be the better offer on another read.

questions.prompt: Why is the faceoff circle only a search area?
questions.explanation: It helps YOU and Navy2 orient, but Gold1's location and the passing lane still decide whether the circle is useful.

scenarios.title: Too close to the carrier
scenarios.objective: Leave room for a teammate while remaining available.
scenarios.briefing: Navy2 has the puck and YOU are only a short step away. Navy3 offers a separate option. Gold1 is ahead. This keep-away activity asks partners to avoid occupying the same small space. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU and Navy2 are close together.
Navy3 has a separate angle.
Gold1 is ahead of Navy2.

questions.prompt: Which navy player is closest to Navy2?
questions.explanation: YOU are two metres from Navy2 in this illustration; Navy3 is farther away.

questions.prompt: What might extra separation give Navy2?
questions.explanation: Separation can offer room and another angle. It cannot guarantee the next pass.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into separate space while keeping Navy2 in view.
questions.explanation: The reference opens a different support angle. Several distances could suit the players; no universal spacing is claimed.

questions.prompt: Arrange a spacing check.

options.text: Notice whether you are crowding them

questions.explanation: This is a coaching suggestion. Staying closer can be useful in other states, so re-check the situation.

questions.prompt: Imagine pressure reaches Navy2 and a short outlet is needed. Should YOU always move farther away?

options.text: Yes, get as far away as possible
No, a nearby clear angle can help
No, stay right beside Navy2 and wait

questions.explanation: Useful distance depends on the pressure and on the route the pass has to travel. Going as far as possible can put YOU out of reach, and staying right beside Navy2 leaves the crowded space this picture starts with.

questions.prompt: Why is more space not the same as going as far away as possible?
questions.explanation: A useful answer connects room with staying available. The source supports near and far support, not one fixed distance.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 skates across to the same side of Navy2 as YOU. What is a useful first response?

options.text: Find a support spot on Navy2's other side
Hold the same spot and wait for the pass
Skate in beside Navy2 for a hand-off

questions.explanation: Check whether Gold1 has actually closed your angle. If so, a clear spot on Navy2's other side may offer something new. Keep enough room for Navy2 to handle the puck. Your first spot can still work if Gold1 cannot reach that lane.

questions.prompt: What two relationships should shape your spacing?
questions.explanation: Spacing is useful when it gives the carrier room and responds to pressure. The scene does not establish a universal measured distance.

questions.prompt: Place YOU on the side of Navy2 away from Gold1, with room for Navy2 to handle the puck.
questions.explanation: Gold1 stands ahead of Navy2 on the other side, so this example sits on the quiet side and the line from the puck runs away from Gold1. It is about four metres from Navy2, which leaves the carrier room while staying inside a short pass. Navy3 still holds a separate angle farther up the ice, and other reachable spots on that side can work.

questions.prompt: How can Navy3 change your support choice?
questions.explanation: Navy3 already offers an angle farther up the ice, so YOU do not need to crowd Navy2. Use where Gold1 is and which lanes are already covered to pick a spot the other navy player is not holding.

scenarios.title: Look beyond the nearest jersey
scenarios.objective: Compare a nearby covered teammate with another support option.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have the puck. Navy2 is nearby, but Gold1 occupies the direct line to Navy2. Navy3 is farther away at another angle; Gold2 is away from that illustrated line. Compare the options before trying a pass. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Navy2 is the nearer teammate.
Gold1 sits on that near line.
Navy3 offers another angle.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is nearer YOU?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is the nearby partner on the same line.

questions.prompt: Where is Gold1 standing in this picture?

options.text: Close to YOU, almost on the line to Navy2
Beside Navy3, far up the ice
Far behind YOU, near the navy end

questions.explanation: Gold1 is two and a half metres from YOU, closer still to the puck, and almost exactly on the line from the puck to Navy2. Gold1 is more than eleven metres from Navy3, and stands ahead of YOU rather than behind.

questions.prompt: What should you compare besides distance?

options.text: Whether a teammate is always closest

questions.explanation: Distance alone does not establish availability.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little to inspect a different passing angle.
questions.explanation: This changes the relationship to both targets. It is exploratory; the final choice still depends on defenders and puck travel.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold2 closes Navy3's line before you pass. What could you do?

options.text: Pass to Navy3 anyway because that was the plan
Watch Gold1 only and stop tracking Gold2

questions.explanation: The suggested preference changes when a line closes. Passing on the old plan sends the puck toward the new pressure, and tracking one defender only hides the change. If Gold2 stops short and the line stays open, Navy3 can still be a good choice.

questions.prompt: Why might the farther teammate be worth a look here?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is close but Gold1 sits on that line. Navy3 is at a different angle, though Gold1 is also near the start of that longer line in this picture, so neither pass is simply open. A useful answer says the far option is worth checking and that moving the puck first can change both angles.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 moves off the line to Navy2 and comes at YOU from the side. What can change?

options.text: The line to Navy2 can open up
Navy2 becomes a worse option every time

questions.explanation: Moving off that line may leave Navy2 available, while Gold1 coming closer gives YOU less time. Check Gold1's reach and the lane before passing; movement alone does not guarantee an opening.

questions.prompt: Which two checks help YOU judge a pass to Navy3?

options.text: Whether Navy3 is ready to receive
Whether Gold1 or Gold2 can reach the passing lane
Whether Navy2 is the closest teammate

questions.explanation: Check the receiver and the whole passing lane. Gold1 is close to the puck and Gold2 is nearer Navy3. Either can affect the pass. Navy2 is another option, but being closest does not decide whether Navy3 is available.

questions.prompt: Place YOU where the puck has more room from Gold1 and both teammates stay ahead of YOU.
questions.explanation: Gold1 is closer to the puck than to YOU, so making room can come before choosing a target. From this example the puck sits about five metres from Gold1 instead of under two, and both navy teammates are still in front. Gold1 can follow, so look again before passing.

questions.prompt: If both teammates were covered, what could YOU do with the puck instead?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A useful reply names something YOU can do without a pass, such as carrying to a new angle, protecting the puck, or waiting for a teammate to move. Nothing in a still picture proves any of those would work.

scenarios.title: Receive, then find the next picture
scenarios.objective: Refresh teammate and pressure information after reception.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have just controlled a short pass near the faceoff circle in the defending end. The earlier pass is not animated. Navy2 now waits toward centre ice; Navy3 waits along the boards. Gold1 is closer to YOU than Gold2. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU control the puck after reception.
YOU are near a faceoff circle.
Navy2 and Navy3 occupy different areas.

questions.prompt: Where did YOU receive the puck?

options.text: Inside the gold goal at the +x end
In the corner behind your own net

questions.explanation: YOU are standing on a faceoff dot in the end navy defends, which is where this practice picture places the reception.

questions.prompt: Which locations are useful to update now?
questions.explanation: Check partners and pressure after reception.

questions.prompt: Arrange one receive-and-read routine.

options.text: Notice the new pressure and support

questions.explanation: This is a simple suggested routine. Experienced players may scan before and during reception too.

questions.prompt: Move YOU a little toward centre ice to inspect the support picture.
questions.explanation: This creates a new angle away from the nearer pressure side. It is not a proven escape path.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy3 leaves the boards before your next action. What should change?

options.text: Keep passing to the old spot

questions.explanation: The relevant target is the actual teammate location, not a memorized board mark.

questions.prompt: What did you need to learn again after receiving?
questions.explanation: Describe the current pressure or a teammate location. The earlier pass does not decide the next read.

questions.prompt: Gold1 stands almost in the line from the puck to Navy2. Which navy option is clearer right now?

options.text: Navy2, because Navy2 is farther up the ice

questions.explanation: The line from the puck to Navy2 runs straight past Gold1, and the shorter line to Navy3 is well clear of Gold1 in this picture. Being farther up the ice does not help if the puck cannot get there. If Gold1 steps across, look again.

questions.prompt: Which two facts about the gold players matter most right now?

options.text: Gold1 stands in the line to Navy2

questions.explanation: Gold1 is both the nearer gold player and the one standing in the lane to Navy2, so Gold1 shapes this decision. Nothing in the picture shows Gold2 beaten; Gold2 is farther up the ice and can still take away the next option.

questions.prompt: Place YOU where there is more room from Gold1 before choosing an option.
questions.explanation: This example creates more room from Gold1 and changes the angles to both navy teammates. Check each lane again before passing: Gold1 can follow or reach into a lane. Another route may work if it keeps the puck controlled.

questions.prompt: Why can the picture change between a pass leaving and the puck arriving?
questions.explanation: Players keep skating while the puck travels, so the teammate and pressure positions when the pass leaves may not be the ones YOU meet. A useful answer names something that could move, such as Gold1 stepping into the lane or Navy2 finding new space. This still frame does not show that movement.

scenarios.title: Handle the puck beside the boards
scenarios.objective: Notice pressure and nearby inside room while carrying.
scenarios.briefing: YOU control the puck beside the boards in the attacking end. Gold1 faces you from the goalward side. Navy2 offers an inside partner near the faceoff circle. This is a puck-control activity, not a checking drill. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU are close to the boards.
Gold1 is on the goalward side.
Navy2 is farther inside the rink.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is farther from the side boards?
questions.explanation: Navy2 stands well inside the rink. YOU are the one close to the side boards, about three metres from them.

questions.prompt: Which two things deserve a look before moving?

options.text: A promise that every route works

questions.explanation: These are the source-supported cues; a safe route is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Explore a little inside space while keeping Navy2 available.
questions.explanation: The reference moves away from the boards and the goalward opponent. Other choices may work; no contact or travel-time result is certified.

questions.prompt: Arrange a careful control check.
questions.explanation: This is one coaching routine, not a forced game answer.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 moves inside instead. Should you keep using the same inside spot?

options.text: Yes, the inside spot is always open
Recheck where Gold1 actually went before deciding
Turn back toward the boards without looking

questions.explanation: The useful space depends on where the pressure actually is. If Gold1 moves inside, that room can close and the board side can open, so the answer comes from looking rather than from a habit.

questions.prompt: How do the boards change the room you can use?
questions.explanation: They bound one side of the space. Discuss inside support or another available route without assuming a guaranteed escape.

questions.prompt: Gold1 stands between YOU and the net. Where does the open route to Navy2 run?

options.text: Away from Gold1, back toward the middle of the ice
Straight through Gold1 toward the net

questions.explanation: Gold1 stands on the net side of the puck, and the line from the puck to Navy2 heads away from Gold1 toward the middle of the ice. Going along the boards past Gold1 skates into the pressure with the boards on your other side. Nothing here proves the pass or the route would be completed.

questions.prompt: What two things happen if YOU keep going toward the corner?

options.text: The boards curve in and the space gets tighter
Gold1 is already near that route

questions.explanation: The boards curve into the corner and Gold1 is nearby. Navy2 is back toward the middle, so continuing toward the corner can make that pass longer. A corner can still help YOU protect the puck; check the pressure and the lane.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 closer to give YOU a short, clear outlet.
questions.explanation: A shorter offer is easier to reach from a tight board-side spot, and this example keeps the line clear of Gold1, who stands on the net side of the puck. Navy2 could also stay wider to stretch the play; that depends on how hard Gold1 presses.

questions.prompt: What would YOU say out loud to Navy2 from this spot?
questions.explanation: YOU have the puck. You could tell Navy2 which side Gold1 is on, ask Navy2 to show a target, or say where YOU can send a pass. Useful talk helps your partner understand the next choice; it does not guarantee the play will work.

scenarios.title: Find pressure before a corner pickup
scenarios.objective: Notice a loose puck, pressure and support before choosing a pickup route.
scenarios.briefing: A loose puck waits in the corner in the attacking end. YOU are nearest it. Gold1 is approaching from the inside of this practice area; Navy2 waits along the boards away from the corner. The approach is stated, not simulated. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The puck is loose in the corner.
Gold1 approaches from inside.
Navy2 offers a board-side partner.

questions.prompt: What is the puck's state at this freeze?
questions.explanation: No owner is assigned and the puck is near the corner.

questions.prompt: What could YOU find before the pickup?

options.text: The result of a pass that has not happened

questions.explanation: Locate pressure and support; do not assume a later result.

questions.prompt: You spotted Gold1 and Navy2 before moving. When should you look for them again?

options.text: Only once the puck is on your stick
Keep checking as you approach and before choosing your first touch
After you send the pass to Navy2

questions.explanation: Gold1 and Navy2 can move while you approach. Keep checking pressure and support along with the puck, so your first touch fits the newest picture. Looking once does not finish the job.

questions.prompt: Show a nearby approach point while keeping the pressure side in mind.
questions.explanation: This example approaches on the board side. It needs coaching and path checks; other angles may work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 moves to the boards side. What should you check again?

options.text: Which side Gold1 is coming from
Only where the puck is sitting
Nothing, because you already looked once

questions.explanation: Check which side Gold1 is coming from now. Finding the puck alone does not tell you where the pressure is. One early look does not cover a later change.

questions.prompt: Why should finding the puck not be your only job here?
questions.explanation: The puck location alone does not reveal Gold1 or the partner option. This is a simple pickup read, not a structured breakout system.

questions.prompt: Navy2 sees Gold1 closing from the inside. What could Navy2 call to help YOU before the pickup?
questions.explanation: A short call such as “Pressure inside; I am along the boards” gives the pressure side and an outlet. YOU still check the play: the call helps the scan and does not replace it.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 wins the puck before YOU, what could Navy2 do?

options.text: Check Gold1’s route and look for a useful passing lane to close
Look toward the Navy net and recover to help defend
Keep waiting in the old spot for a pass from YOU

questions.explanation: Gold1 now has possession, so Navy2’s job changes from offering an outlet to helping defend. Recovering or closing an available lane can help; if Navy2 can reach the puck under control, challenging it may also fit.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to offer a shorter pass along the boards once YOU gain control.
questions.explanation: The example brings Navy2 closer along the board side while staying away from Gold1’s inside approach. A shorter outlet can help after the pickup, but Navy2 must keep checking whether Gold1 can close the lane.

questions.prompt: The puck is near where the side boards curve around the end of the rink. What do we call this area?
questions.explanation: This is the corner. The slot is the middle space in front of the net; the point is near the attacking blue line. Naming the corner helps a teammate understand where the pickup is happening.

scenarios.title: Pressure before a wall reception
scenarios.objective: Read the pressure side before a planned pass reaches the wall.
scenarios.briefing: Navy2 holds the puck and plans a pass to YOU near the boards. Gold1 approaches from the circle side; Navy3 is a second navy option along the wall. This freeze is before the pass, so YOU cannot shoot or carry the puck yet. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The puck still belongs to Navy2.
YOU wait near the boards.
Gold1 approaches from the circle side.

questions.prompt: Do YOU control the puck at this freeze?

options.text: No, the puck is loose on the ice

questions.explanation: Navy2 is still the puck owner in this picture, so this is the moment before the planned reception. The puck is not loose.

questions.prompt: What can YOU notice before reception?
questions.explanation: Pressure and support are available information. A future shot is not established.

questions.prompt: Arrange this declared two-stage activity.

options.text: Read while Navy2 has the puck
Receive if the planned pass is made

questions.explanation: The reception is conditional, and the next action depends on the new state.

questions.prompt: Show a slightly different receiving angle near the boards.
questions.explanation: The reference changes the approach angle. It is a suggestion, not proof the pass will arrive.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 comes along the boards instead. What is a useful response?

options.text: Use the old plan without looking

questions.explanation: A different pressure side may call for a different touch or route.

questions.prompt: What can you do before the puck is yours?
questions.explanation: Look, communicate and prepare an available target. A puck action must wait for actual control.

questions.prompt: Imagine YOU receive the pass and Gold1 then covers the line back to Navy2. What can YOU do?

options.text: Carry to a new angle and check the pass to Navy2 again
Send it back on the covered line anyway
Stand still and wait for Navy2 to skate to YOU

questions.explanation: Imagine YOU have received the puck. YOU are now the carrier. A controlled move can change your passing angle to Navy2, but check Gold1 again before sending it. Navy3 may also offer a clear pass, or YOU may need to protect the puck.

questions.prompt: Which two things does this picture actually show?

options.text: Gold1 is nearer the middle of the ice than YOU
The pass has already been made

questions.explanation: Navy2 is the puck owner, and Gold1 stands nearer the middle of the ice while YOU wait closer to the boards. The pass has not happened; this freeze is before it.

questions.prompt: Place YOU where Navy2 would have a new option away from Gold1, after a pass back.
questions.explanation: This asks YOU to imagine the pass and the return. From this example Navy2 has an offer of about five metres on the board side, and the line to it stays well away from Gold1, who is nearer the middle. Other clear spots can work, and if Gold1 follows YOU the picture changes again.

questions.prompt: If YOU pass the puck back to Navy2, why would YOU keep skating?
questions.explanation: A useful answer says a player who stops can be easier to cover, and that moving gives the carrier a new option. This picture is the moment before the first pass, so the return pass is something to imagine rather than something shown.

scenarios.title: A waiting pass that is blocked
scenarios.objective: Recognize a blocked intended pass and keep alternatives open.
scenarios.briefing: YOU hold the puck near centre ice. Navy2 is waiting ahead, but Gold1 stands on the intended pass line. Navy3 offers a different angle. The coach permits carrying or another pass; there is no must-pass rule. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Gold1 occupies the line to Navy2.
Navy3 offers another direction.
The activity allows more than one action.

questions.prompt: Who stands on the intended line to Navy2?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is between the carrier and Navy2 on the same line.

questions.prompt: Which actions can be explored under this activity rule?
questions.explanation: The briefing allows carrying or another pass. Availability still needs review.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to explore room away from the blocked line.
questions.explanation: This changes the angle to the options. It does not prove that Gold1 will stay fixed during a real carry.

questions.prompt: Arrange one response to a blocked plan.

options.text: Notice the lane has a defender
Choose after checking the new picture

questions.explanation: This avoids treating the first plan as an instruction that must be completed.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 leaves Navy2's line while Navy2 stays available. Could Navy2 become an option again?

options.text: Yes, if a new check shows the lane is clear
Only if Navy2 first skates to a different spot
No, a first plan that gets blocked is finished for that shift

questions.explanation: Availability depends on the lane right now, not on a permanent label. Navy2 does not have to move for the lane to open, and a blocked first plan is not finished; what matters is what the next look shows.

questions.prompt: Why is changing your first plan sometimes useful?
questions.explanation: A relevant answer connects the changed lane with another visible option, while allowing more than one reasonable choice.

questions.prompt: Gold1 stays on the line to Navy2. Which option does this picture already offer?

options.text: A pass toward Navy3 on the other angle
A pass through Gold1 to Navy2
Waiting until Navy2's line opens on its own

questions.explanation: Navy3 stands on a different angle from the covered line to Navy2, so that is an option this picture offers, and the briefing also allows a short carry. A pass through Gold1 can give the opponent a chance to win the puck. Waiting can work if Gold1 is already leaving, but a still picture does not show that. Check the lane again before passing, because Navy3 can be covered as well.

questions.prompt: Which of these can YOU actually see in this picture?

options.text: Navy3 stands on a different angle from Navy2
Gold1 is already moving toward YOU

questions.explanation: The puck owner and the two navy angles are drawn in the picture. Nothing in a freeze shows a player moving, so Gold1's next move is not a fact yet.

questions.prompt: Who owns the puck before F1 releases it?
questions.explanation: The puck owner is stated as F1; the receiving picture does not transfer possession early.

questions.prompt: Which two observations shape a useful receiving spot?

options.text: Whether D1 can close the inside shoulder
Whether F1 can reach the new spot cleanly
Whether F2 is up ice regardless of the lane

questions.explanation: D1’s position and F1’s passing lane shape the receiving target. Scan F2’s possible continuation too, without assuming the next pass is open.

questions.prompt: Arrange this receiving decision.

options.text: Present a reachable target to F1
Receive under control and choose the next option

questions.explanation: The scan informs the target, then the touch can be adjusted to the pressure and the available continuation.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a receiving point with more separation from D1 and a visible lane from F1.
questions.explanation: This point changes the angle from F1 and gives D1 a different relationship; the pass still needs to be reachable.

questions.prompt: D1 steps into your inside shoulder as F1 releases. Which reception fits the changed cue?

options.text: Open your body to protect the puck and keep a return option
Turn fully up ice before the puck arrives
Demand the same forward turn even if the lane is covered

questions.explanation: D1 has removed the easy inside turn, so a protected touch and a conditional return preserve more choices.

questions.prompt: Why can a wider receiving angle help here, and what would make you change it?
questions.explanation: A wider angle can separate YOU from D1 while preserving F1's lane. Change it if D1 follows or F1 loses a clean route, then re-offer a reachable option.

scenarios.title: Re-offer after the first lane is covered
scenarios.objective: Change the support relationship when a defender stays in the original passing line.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x). F1 has the puck just inside the attacking zone. YOU are farther up ice on the same lateral line, with D1 between you. F2 is wide on the other side and may become useful if D1 follows a new support angle.
cues: D1 sits between F1 and YOU.
F2 is wide on the far side.
A new angle may change which teammate becomes available.

Whether F1 can still see and reach YOU
Whether the same route is still blocked after you move

questions.explanation: Check whether D1 follows, whether F1 can still see and reach YOU, and whether the old route is still blocked. Those three observations tell you whether the changed angle helped.

options.text: Check F1, D1 and F2 again

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 follows your move toward the middle. What is worth checking?

options.text: The space D1 left for F2 or another F1 lane
The original lane as if D1 stayed still
A pass to YOU no matter where F1 looks

questions.explanation: D1's movement can change another relationship. Scan F2 and any newly open lane before deciding where to support.

questions.prompt: Explain how your movement can help F1 even if the puck never comes to you.
questions.explanation: Moving D1 can open F2 or a carrier lane. Call the new space, keep F1 in view, and be ready to adjust again if the defender recovers.

D1 shades the old return line.
F1 is a visible alternate support player.

questions.prompt: Which two details should shape your next support spot?

options.text: D1's relationship to the old return line
Where the earlier pass started, without checking the new carrier

questions.explanation: F2 and D1 help you judge whether to change your support angle. Recheck the available space; a return pass is only one possible continuation.

questions.prompt: What can your support accomplish when F2 keeps the puck?
questions.explanation: It can pull D1, offer a second lane, or protect F2's next option. Describe the named space and make the benefit conditional on D1's response.
